segs.text: Section thirty two. Immunologic and nonimmunologic reactions, risk factors, and hypersensitivity types. The more drugs given, the more likely an adverse drug reaction. Hospitalized patients on fewer than six drugs: five percent; on more than fifteen drugs: more than forty percent. Ambulatory patients, who usually take fewer drugs, sit at about twenty percent. Separately, a number of widely used drugs cause ninety percent of all reactions, and she named opioids, cardiac medications and diabetes medications as the big three.

Reactions fall into two groups: nonimmunologic reactions are predictable, immunologic reactions often are not. Predictable nonimmunologic examples: dry mouth from antihistamines, liver toxicity from methotrexate, seizure from excessive lidocaine. But three nonimmunologic kinds are unpredictable. Pseudoallergic, such as the itch from radiocontrast dye, feels allergic but is the drug itself. Idiosyncratic, such as hemolytic anemia after primaquine in G six P D deficiency. And intolerance, whose classic example is tinnitus, ringing in the ears, after a single small dose of aspirin.

Patient risk factors split by group. Female gender, H I V infection, and lupus are risk factors for both kinds of reaction. Renal insufficiency, liver disease, alcoholism and polypharmacy belong to general, nonimmune reactions. Asthma, previous hypersensitivity to a chemically related drug, and specific genetic polymorphisms are risk factors only for immune, hypersensitivity reactions.

What a layperson calls a drug allergy is properly a hypersensitivity reaction. The Gell and Coombs classification gives four types, and timing is the key. Type one is mediated by the antibody I g E: the drug I g E complex binds mast cells and releases histamine, within minutes to hours. Type two is cytotoxic, variable timing. Type three deposits drug antibody complexes in tissue, causing serum sickness one to three weeks later. Type four is delayed and cell mediated: the drug must be presented to T cells and cytokines released, so it appears two to seven days after skin exposure, as in contact dermatitis. More than one type can occur at once, and a reaction that looks like immune hypersensitivity may actually be idiosyncratic.

The type changes treatment. Type one works through histamine, so antihistamines are the main treatment, then steroids. The other types work through antibodies against cells, immune complexes or T cells, so steroids are used, and possibly other therapies.
Stevens Johnson syndrome is painful and dangerous, can involve the mouth and mucosal tract, and the skin can come off. Carbamazepine puts people with a certain H L A B variant at risk.
